svg.text: eleven marks, their function, and their literary example

g.text: QUESTION MARK — ends a direct question.
○ "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" (Shakespeare, Sonnet 18)
EXCLAMATION MARK — strong emotion or emphasis.
SEMICOLON — joins closely related independent clauses.
○ "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;" (Yeats, The Second Coming)
COLON — introduces lists, explanations, or quotations.
○ "To be, or not to be: that is the question." (Shakespeare, Hamlet)
EM DASH — break in thought; stronger than commas/parens.
○ "Because I could not stop for Death —" (Dickinson)
QUOTATION MARKS — enclose direct speech / quoted matter.
HYPHEN — joins compound modifiers, numbers, prefixes.
Before noun: "well-known author" — after: "author is well known"
○ "...died in a freak accident (picnic, lightning)..." (Nabokov, Lolita)
ELLIPSIS — omitted words, or a trailing-off in dialogue.
○ "So we beat on, boats against the current…" (Fitzgerald, Gatsby)

svg.text: five contexts, plus the serial comma

g.text: ○ She bought apples, oranges, and bananas.
○ "Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered..." (Poe, The Raven)
○ George, when a little boy, had a hatchet given him.
○ It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks struck thirteen.
○ Reader, I married him. (Brontë, Jane Eyre)
Style choice, not a rule — apply it consistently. Comma splice → §7.4.
"to my parents, Ayn Rand and God" vs "...Ayn Rand, and God"
its, yours, theirs, ours, hers, his.
pronoun "I"; first word of quoted speech.
○ "Toto, I've a feeling we're not in Kansas anymore."
prepositions — unless first or last word.
○ "The Cat in the Hat" / "War and Peace"
British: inside only if part of the quote

svg.text: all fourteen, §7.1–7.14 — structural faults diagrammed, lexical faults as ✗/✓

g.text: correct: reword so "I" is the subject present.
correct: move the modifier beside its target.
correct: reposition to force one reading.
Implied subject never appears; attaches to whatever subject is supplied.
✗ Running late, the bus left without me.
✓ Running late, I found the bus had already left.
Placed too far from the word it describes; seems to modify something else.
✗ She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.
✓ She served the children sandwiches on paper plates.
Both concords are correct — the traditions differ (5.1.1). The fault is mixing them.
✓ The team are winning. notional concord, BrE — the team as its members
✓ The team is winning. grammatical concord, AmE — the team as one unit
✗ The team are winning, and it has scored twice. — one sentence, two concords
Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone, or by no punctuation.
A phrase or dependent clause punctuated as a complete sentence.
Because the dog barked loudly all night.
Mixing grammatical forms within a list, comparison, or coordination.
Could point to more than one antecedent, or to no specific noun at all.
✓ reword: repeat the noun — "the car was badly damaged."
Sentence begins with one structure and shifts to an incompatible one.
✗ By studying every night is how she passed the exam.
✓ By studying every night, she passed the exam.
Wrong case in a compound subject/object, or after a preposition.
✗ Me and him went to the store.
✓ He and I went to the store.
Confusing a contraction (it's = it is) with its possessive homophone.
Test: expand it — "the dog wagged it is tail" fails, so its is required.
Combining more/most with a form already inflected for comparison.
✗ This was the most unkindest cut of all. (Shakespeare — deliberate)
✓ This was the unkindest cut of all. — one degree marker
Sits between two readings, leaving the sentence genuinely ambiguous.
✗ Students who revise essays regularly improve their writing.
✓ Students who regularly revise essays improve their writing.
Subject and predicate cannot logically combine, despite well-formed syntax.
✗ Arachnophobia is when someone fears spiders.
✓ Arachnophobia is the fear of spiders.
An unmotivated change of grammatical person or number mid-sentence.
✗ I enjoy hiking because you can see nature up close.
✓ I enjoy hiking because I can see nature up close.
